title: Sommelier Reasoning: advanced deductive method
description: An advanced level to connect climate, soil, winemaking, and sensory evidence with professional logic.

lessons.title: Climate and ripening
lessons.intro: Climate is the key structural variable: it affects sugar, acidity, and phenolic maturity.
lessons.final: You can now use acidity, alcohol, and fruit profile as climate clues.

slides.title: Three ripeness dimensions
paragraphs: Technological ripeness: sugar accumulation and potential alcohol.
Phenolic ripeness: tannin and color compound evolution.
Aromatic ripeness: development of varietal and fermentative aromas.

slides.title: Deductive logic
paragraphs: High acidity with moderate alcohol often suggests cooler conditions.
Riper fruit with higher alcohol often suggests warmer conditions or later picking.

answers: Build a hypothesis to verify with other clues

lessons.title: Soil, water, and vigor
lessons.intro: Soil does not directly give flavors: it controls water balance, vigor, and ripening rhythm.
lessons.final: You can evaluate how water availability and vigor shape concentration and style.

slides.title: Real soil function
paragraphs: Soil influences drainage, water reserve, and root development.
The vine responds by changing vegetative vigor and crop balance.

slides.title: Wine impact
paragraphs: Excess water can dilute aroma and phenolic compounds.
Moderate, controlled stress can improve concentration and precision.

lessons.title: Extraction: maceration and tannin
lessons.intro: Maceration length and technique define how much structure is extracted from skins and seeds.
lessons.final: You can connect extraction choices to color, tannin profile, and drinkability.

slides.title: What is extracted
paragraphs: Skins contribute color compounds and part of the tannin load.
Seeds may add greener tannins if maturity is not complete.

slides.title: Operational choices
paragraphs: Short maceration tends toward lighter, fruit-forward styles.
Longer and more intense extraction increases structure and potential astringency.

lessons.title: Fermentation and temperature
lessons.intro: Fermentation temperature shapes aromatic profile, kinetics, and stability.
lessons.final: You can explain how fermentation decisions influence style and aromatic clarity.

slides.title: Temperature-aroma link
paragraphs: Cooler fermentation often preserves more primary aromas in white wines.
Warmer red fermentations can improve extraction and complexity if controlled.

slides.title: Risks and goals
paragraphs: Poor thermal control can create off-aromas or fermentation issues.
Professional target: align desired style with a coherent cellar protocol.

lessons.title: Aging vessels: steel, oak, concrete
lessons.intro: Vessel choice is not neutral: it affects oxygen exchange, texture, and final aromatic profile.
lessons.final: You can identify the main effects of different aging vessels.

slides.title: Three approaches
paragraphs: Steel: aromatic neutrality and freshness protection.
Oak: gradual oxygen exchange plus possible aromatic contribution.
Concrete: thermal inertia and moderate exchange without obvious oak notes.

slides.title: Deductive application
paragraphs: Vanilla, sweet spice, and broader texture may suggest oak influence.
Tighter, linear profiles often suggest steel or reductive handling.

lessons.title: Full deductive method
lessons.intro: Thinking like a sommelier means building progressive hypotheses and validating them coherently.
lessons.final: Advanced level complete: you now reason through clues, connections, and verification.

slides.title: Operational sequence
paragraphs: Observe: intensity, hue, and consistency.
Smell: aroma families, intensity, and cleanliness.
Taste: sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol, body, and finish.

slides.title: From clue to conclusion
paragraphs: No single clue is enough; convergence is what matters.
Professional practice avoids shortcuts: hypothesize, verify, and manage uncertainty.
